summary: This standards-track RFC defines procedures for using Seamless BFD in IPv4, IPv6 and MPLS environments.

plainLanguage.summary: Step-by-step instructions for using quick path checks in the three main network types.

questions: how does an s-bfd reflector reply
subtitle: The UDP port numbers and packet rules that let Seamless BFD run over IPv4, IPv6 and MPLS.

tldr.problem: Seamless BFD (S-BFD) is a general way to check that a path to a remote node works, but it needs concrete rules for how its packets travel over IPv4, IPv6 and MPLS.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7881 assigns UDP port 7784 to S-BFD control packets, reuses port 3785 for S-BFD Echo, and specifies the IP, UDP and label-stack header values for the initiator and the reflector.
tldr.outcome: Implementations in these environments can interoperate. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7881 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2016. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata for this RFC, and it builds on RFC 7880.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (S-BFD), defined in RFC 7880, is a generalized mechanism that lets network nodes perform continuity checks to remote entities without the session setup of classical BFD. RFC 7881 supplies the procedures for using it in IPv4, IPv6 and MPLS environments.

The reader is expected to know IP, BFD (RFC 5880), MPLS BFD (RFC 5884) and S-BFD. The document does not distinguish single-hop from multi-hop S-BFD; both are supported.
sections.plainLanguage: S-BFD is a quick way to ask 'can I still reach you?'. This document says exactly how to send that question on common kinds of networks.

sections.title: UDP Ports
sections.content:
A new UDP port, 7784, is defined for S-BFD control packets. A SBFDReflector session MUST listen on port 7784, and SBFDInitiator sessions MUST send control packets with destination port 7784. The initiator's source port can be any port except 7784. The same source port MUST be used for all packets of one initiator session, and it is unique among all initiator sessions on the system. The initiator listens for reflected packets at that source port.

The S-BFD Echo function uses the BFD Echo port from RFC 5881, port 3785. Initiators MUST send Echo packets with destination port 3785. The source port and the Echo procedures themselves are outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Ports are like door numbers. Questions go to door 7784, and the answer comes back to whichever door the asker used, which is never 7784.

sections.title: Demultiplexing Control Packets
sections.content:
Received S-BFD control packets are sorted using the destination UDP port, following Section 7.1 of RFC 7880. The same procedure runs on both initiator and reflector.

If the port is 7784, the packet is for a reflector, and the node MUST look up a reflector session using the Your Discriminator field in the table of S-BFD discriminators. If the port is not 7784 but the packet is for an initiator, the node MUST look up an initiator session using Your Discriminator in the table of BFD discriminators, and SHOULD check that the destination IP address is its own. If the packet belongs to a classical BFD session, the procedures of RFC 5880 apply.
sections.plainLanguage: When a message arrives, the door number says whether it is a question or an answer, and a name tag inside says which exact desk should get it.

sections.title: Initiator Procedures
sections.content:
S-BFD control packets carry an IP header, a UDP header and a BFD control packet. When they are explicitly label switched (sent on a specific LSP rather than IP routed), a label stack is prepended. The BFD control header values come from RFC 7880.

For all packets, the source IP address MUST be a local address expected to be routable by the target (not an IPv6 link-local address when the target is several hops away), the UDP destination port MUST be 7784, and the UDP source port MUST NOT be 7784.

For IP-routed packets, the destination address MUST be an address of the target and the TTL or Hop Limit SHOULD be 255. For explicitly label-switched packets, the packet MUST carry the label stack expected to reach the target, the topmost label's TTL SHOULD be 255, the destination IP address MUST come from 127/8 for IPv4 or 0:0:0:0:0:ffff:7f00:0/104 for IPv6 as per RFC 5884, and the IP TTL or Hop Limit MUST be 1.

The RFC uses the word target rather than remote entity on purpose. An initiator can set Your Discriminator and TTL carefully to test the path toward a target but destined to a transit node, using TTL expiry. For this, responders MUST let received S-BFD control packets on the TTL expiry exception path reach the matching reflector session, as is existing practice for OAM packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The asker writes its own address on the envelope, aims at door 7784, and gives it plenty of travel time. If it uses a special tunnel, it uses a special address so the message stays on that tunnel.

sections.title: Reflector Procedures
sections.content:
The reflector sends its replies back by normal IP routing, with an IP header, a UDP header and a BFD control header. If a reflector receives a packet whose UDP source port is 7784, it MUST discard it.

For each reply, the destination IP address MUST be copied from the source address of the received packet. The source IP address MUST be a local address the initiator expects to see (again not IPv6 link-local if the initiator is several hops away) and SHOULD be copied from the destination address of the received packet, except when that is from 127/8 or 0:0:0:0:0:ffff:7f00:0/104. The TTL or Hop Limit MUST be 255. The UDP ports are swapped: the destination port is copied from the received source port, and the source port from the received destination port.
sections.plainLanguage: The answerer flips the envelope: it sends the reply to the sender's address and door, from the door the question came in on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Security considerations for S-BFD are in RFC 7880. RFC 7881 adds three measures. Implementations MUST be able to filter on the source IP addresses of received S-BFD control packets (see RFC 2827). They MUST NOT act on control packets from source Martian addresses, meaning addresses whose return traffic would not be routed back to the sender by the current forwarding tables. And they MUST make sure reflected packets have a reachable target, such as a reachable destination IP address.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not answer letters with fake return addresses, and only reply to addresses you can actually reach.

sections.title: IANA Port Assignment
sections.content: IANA allocated port 7784 from the Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry. The entry has service name s-bfd, transport protocol UDP, the IESG as assignee, the IETF Chair as contact, and the description 'Seamless Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (S-BFD)', with RFC 7881 as the reference.
sections.plainLanguage: Door number 7784 is now officially reserved for this kind of check.
